items.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs Trail Blazers, November 21, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
As we all know, Madison Square Garden isn’t just the most glorious gymnasium on the planet and revered in the world of sports; it’s also famous for the long list of famous musicians who have performed under its unique bicycle-wheel ceiling. Now the Portland Trail Blazers are dropping by for a quick game of hoops on Saturday night, but they might actually be the one franchise that would be adept at bringing out the microphones as well. I mean, who wouldn’t want to hear the newest rendition of all-timers like or ?!

Not to disappoint anybody, but the days of Terry Porter and those shiny lycra dance outfits of the Blazers cheerleaders that would have made Cory Everson proud are long gone. Today’s Rip City Rascals (coming in at 10-5) have their own way of entertaining a crowd, though, which is more than many would have expected before the season. With the return of Damian Lillard and a highly questionable move for “Pistol Petey” Ja Morant, the Blazers looked to be about five years late to the modern NBA party but atleast early it turns out they are anything but.

Portland is fun under new coach Micah Nori

New head coach Micah Nori is making one of the more funky-looking rosters in the Association work so far, and he does it with a very modern, analytical approach. The Blazers shoot and make way more threes than their opponents (outscoring them by about 12+ points from beyond the arc), defend downtown better than 25 other teams in the NBA, and make sure Tony Brothers and his brothers-in-arms in the striped shirts have a living by drawing the second most fouls in the league.

Most of those foul numbers might be attributed to Deni Avdija. Only Luka from the Lakers and that feaky Greek in Miami stand at the charity stripe more frequently than the Israeli All-Star from Portland, leading to some fans questioning the ethics in his basketball bravado. But make no mistake about it, he is a serious talent, big-bodied and confident with a well-rounded game that can give every opponent problems. If he will be of any concern to the Knicks is not clear yet though; Avdija missed Portland’s last two with a foot injury and figures to be a game-time decision.

But even without Avdija, Portland (road record 7-3) will present a very interesting matchup for your Knickerbockers. Damian Lillard seems to be rejuvenated after his Achilles injury, and a lot about his game feels a bit more wholesome in the jersey in which he always belonged. Behind him you have a Jrue Holiday coming off the bench, probably one of the more professional, classy guys you can find in the NBA these days. Cheekily, he also still packs quite a punch in his game, giving Nori first-class playmaking, tough D, and leadership in spades. If you think rattling these two old wily pros might get you anywhere, think again.

Superior depth could be a factor for Knicks

You could have more luck with some of the younger Blazers, but many of them bring certain elite skills to the table, too. Belgian baller Toumani Camara is one of the best defenders in the entire league, long, lanky, and extremely athletic. Seemingly plodding big man Donovan Clingan is getting more mobile by the minute and still hasn’t lost his knack for gobbling up boards like a motivated Moses Malone did back in the day. Sidy Cissoko is another promising young wing, and former number two overall pick Scoot Henderson, while having a nightmarish season overall, can still break out for a big one as he did against Milwaukee the other night with 27 points.

What all those Blazers have in common is that they buy into Nori’s system so far and operate with a clear-cut plan on the shiny hardwood. They extend their defense, making it hard to find anything downtown but also possible to do some damage in the midrange. On offense, they move the ball well, play five-out as much as they can (using Clingan as a high screen setter), and rely on balanced scoring night in and night out. It’s a good formula, especially without Ja Morant, who has missed all but four games with a hamstring injury so far this year. The Knicks will have to touch the paint plenty to get that Portland defense moving, and they have to attack Lillard whenever possible on that end. Their superior depth could be a factor as well.

If the Blazers then throw a curveball and try to actually upend the Knicks’ three-game winning streak by dragging them into a singing competition after all? No need to worry – we still got !

Who: Portland Trail Blazers (10-5) at New York Knicks (9-6)Date: Saturday, November 21, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I was raised by Wolves’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
I thought yesterday’s game was over by the end of the third quarter…

…only for these fools to nearly drop it. Good thing, they did not.

Here’s a bunch of quotes coming off Minnesota as the boys return home once and for all.

On finishing the road trip with a victory over Minnesota:

“Great to finish off a road trip, getting a win in a pretty tough environment by a well-coached team. It’ll make the plane ride a little bit better going home.”

On the Knicks’ fourth-quarter offensive collapse against the Timberwolves:

“Our execution the first three quarters was at a pretty high level against this team. And then you give them credit. Fourth quarter, they did a phenomenal job defensively, kind of bogged us down. The ball and the pace offensively in the frontcourt wasn’t popping like it was the first three quarters.”

On the Knicks winning the battle for loose balls despite struggling offensively in the fourth quarter:

“The thing that saved us was winning the 50-50 ballgame. We were 13-for-14 in that area, and that was huge for us because we had trouble scoring in the fourth.”

On beating his former team as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

“I was raised by Wolves, but it was Knicks in 5 at the end.”

On why the Knicks don’t need to win games convincingly:

“For ‘Dancing with the Stars.’ For us, at the end of the day, as long as we win, this team is just trying to stack the number on the left side.”

On the importance of winning games in different ways:

“If you wanna win a championship, you gotta be ready to win in any way possible, because you never know what the game will be.”

On his uncertain contract situation and remaining focused on his responsibilities to the Knicks:

“I got a job to do, at the end of the day. I gotta come here and put that jersey on and do what’s best for my brothers and the guys they have in my locker room. So, I’m just here to do my job.”

On refusing to let his contract situation distract him from performing:

“I gotta put that jersey on and put the best performance out there for my teammates. So, that’s all I really think about.”

On his emotional attachment to Minnesota:

“I still have so much love for this place. It doesn’t go away. I think it’s actually grown as I’ve been away. I think that, even for me and my dad, we were just driving around the city and just going to places. We went to eat at a spot we love to go here. It always hits home. This is the last place that I got to play basketball with my mom. I got to see the kids be young before now. Jolani, my niece, who was in my rookie of the year photo actually in here, she was a baby, and now she’s in high school. It’s a different part of life, but it’s a part of life that I really enjoy.”

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion:

“It’s always great to be home and to be back here. Nine years of my life, some amazing years, amazing moments. Yeah, it’s special to be back. Obviously, it’s bittersweet to come back with a championship because I wanted to win it here so bad for the city, for Minneapolis, for Minnesota, for all the people who haven’t seen an NBA championship here. But it’s great to be able to come back and to be able to see friends, people I call family here.”

On the release of the new Grand Theft Auto game and his excitement to play it:

“I haven’t played the game yet, but I’ve heard it’s a hell of a game. So shout-out to Rockstar [Games] and 2K and Take-Two [Interactive]; they did a good job with that one. It’s fun, man. The world is taken over by ‘GTA,’ as it rightfully should be.”

On his Grand Theft Alvarado nickname and his history with the video game:

“I was a big fan of it before my name. It was just a cool name that I had, so it makes it even better when I play the new one. Got the name for it; now, play the game.”

On how much his life has changed since GTA V dropped:

“Thirteen years ago, I wouldn’t even be talking to you, I promise you that. It’s a long journey, fun journey, one hell of a ride. Still with it.”

On the Knicks nearly blowing their lead against Minnesota:

“It was hectic. We gotta get better at finishing a game like that. But it’s a win, 3-1 on the road trip. We’ll take it.”

On the criticism Karl-Anthony Towns faced during his Timberwolves years:

“Particularly when he started his playoff journey, how much flak he had gotten.”

On Towns leading the Wolves to the Western Conference Finals:

“We don’t do it without him in all facets of the game, whether it be his defense in the Phoenix series, the only guy who held us in the game in Game 7 in Denver when we had nothing else going until we could find it in the second half. Those are the little moments that spring to mind. There are many others along the way. And he kind of grew into that and then was able to build on that with an experienced team where he fit into in New York.”

On watching Towns succeed in the Knicks’ championship run:

“It was fun to see him at the heart of it, too. Especially as they were kind of tweaking their offense going along and all of his skills came to the surface through that.”

On the similarities between Towns and LaMelo Ball:

“They play with a lot of expression to their game and people interpret that or they don’t like that. But it doesn’t mean that A) they’re not super talented players, of course, and B) they can’t play winning basketball. Sometimes it’s as much of the environment that people might be judging them unfairly through, if that makes sense.

“They both are really selfless in the way that they play. But maybe some of their expressions and the way that they carry themselves on the court draws a lot of attention and they get judged unfairly for that, too. They’re actually incredibly selfless. They both play with a lot of joy.

“They’re incredible people. Just great teammates, fun to be around, always bring the same energy every day. Very coachable.”

items.title: Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: “3 straight on the road, what’s up…”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
LaMelo Ball hit one of his patented three-pointers from the left elbow early in the third quarter against the New York Knicks last night and as the crowd cheered, he proceeded to jog back on defense. Of course, the only not totally broken Ball brother couldn’t let the moment pass without completely indulging himself into a thoroughly scripted “ice in the veins”-gesture that feels as original these days as a two-handed set shot. Just a moment later Josh Hart rained on the parade, running directly by Vanilla Ball’s D and finishing an easy backdoor cut with a simple layup. And just like that the Knicks were up 14 again, ignoring the protocol of how cutting a deficit to 12 in a game where your team got handsomely dominated up to that point needs to be celebrated.

It feels good to root for a professional team, doesn’t it? It will allow you to say things like Real Clydes Wear Plaid shared in the and which I unapologetically stole for the headline of this recap. The Knicks won their third game in a row at Minnesota last night and they probably made it a lot harder than it needed to be. Their opponents certainly had something to do with it, no matter how ill-advised some individual emotions might have been. The Timberwolves can play tremendous defense, are as long as those trees in their logo and have an aggression you could certainly link to that name-giving animal of them. They got a good albeit cranky coach, a proven system, years of winning experience. Yet in the end they also got LaMelo Ball now.

Knicks hold off Minnesota’s late rally

We get that he is a talented, at times iconic passer; we also get that he has found his footing fairly well on the frozen tundra near the Great Lakes so far. But we really can’t get convinced that you can ever really win big with a “talent” like that. His play can remind one of the game young kids play before they really get a hang of Dr. Naismith’s rules. They also take two steps before every dribble, then four after they pick the ball up. They also couldn’t care less about a repetitive shooting motion or dribbling the ball without palming it every time. With the kids it’s okay and fun, we let them discover themselves as players and excuse it. But Lamborghini LaMelo should be held to a different standard, he is supposed to be a professional NBA player after all.

Luckily for the Knicks, they got plenty of real pros on their roster, guys who truly care about winning and treat their profession like it means something – not only to them but to others. It certainly seemed that way when they played most of the game last night with a level of calmness and concentration that has been a hallmark of theirs ever since they went on that beautiful championship run last year. But despite all their dominance over that two-month stretch in the playoffs, you can’t ignore that they are a team with plenty of cracks in their armor, many of which showed themselves last night as well. It’s the kind of weakness that are often the reason for the Bockers falling behind big only to have the opportunity to stage their beloved monumental comebacks later on.

Knicks’ defense wins it in the end

Yesterday the Knicks offense completely bogged down late when Minnesota went to more switching on D (raise your hand if you’ve seen that before), neutralizing all the beautiful team basketball that helped the Gotham Gang run up an almost 20-point lead earlier. Not even Karl-Anthony Towns, once again mesmerizing for most of the night against a traditional five at his old stomping grounds, couldn’t regain his first-half form. Maybe he rode the pine a little long, Mr. Brown? Well, you can’t play him all 48, we get it. A lineup that included Jose Alvarado, Andre Drummond and Josh Hart was still an interesting choice, to say the least. For all the individual chops it’s quite a load for Jalen Brunson to carry that group offensively, it almost feels like him heaving big AD up K2 or some other majestic mountain. It might get you to the summit against certain defenses but considering some defenses are as long and physical as the Wolf Pack, it can also get cold rather quickly. Especially when Brunson still hasn’t found his touch inside the paint yet.

That New York could still pull it out in the end is a testament to timely plays and a gritty, opportunistic defense that at no point in the game relented to the physically imposing Wolves coming at them. When LaMelo Ball couldn’t find someone open downtown, the canines’ only plan was to ram their oversized combo forwards ahead. It worked here or there but never consistently. Watch out, there’s an extended arm coming at you – boom, another offensive foul! It’s an interesting yet understandable choice by the league to make the off arm a point of emphasis this year (sorry, SGA). Why didn’t they do the same for palming the basketball or taking more steps than a dressage horse? Your guess is as good as mine.

For the moment, though, let us not worry about it – there is a win to be celebrated. For all we know though, our guys are probably watching some film right now and preparing for their next opponent (Portland on Saturday). Maybe they are also speeding race cars through some busy pedestrian zone or practice their one-legged step-back fadeaway jumper that has netted them less than 42 percent shooting for their career?

Nah, we leave that to the guy with ice in his veins.

items.title: Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: Scenes from a beautiful game with a funky tail
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Timberwolves (11-5) have been the talk of the West, especially with their level of success given the absence of star guard Anthony Edwards (knee). Coach Chris Finch has his crew chucking up 116.7 points per game while also leading the league in rebounding and fielding the top defense. So far this season, the Wolves have held every opponent to under 50% from the floor—and they would again tonight. New York (9-6) knew the trouble that awaited them as they squared off with their first Western Conference team of the season. The game started with runs in either direction, but the Knicks gained steam and took a 15-point lead into halftime. In the third quarter, Minnesota chipped away at the lead, and Jaden McDaniels led the doggies on a rally in the fourth quarter to cut the lead to three with a scant few minutes left. But neither team could buy a bucket down the stretch. The Knicks went scoreless for the final three and a half minutes, the T’Wolves missed on everything, and the visitors escaped with a 102-99 victory.

That’s the lowest score for the Wolves this season. Take a bow, fellas.

On a first-quarter drive, LaMelo Ball (your favorite Ball brother?) swiped an arm across Jalen Brunson’s face. Cap was rattled by it and subbed out around the nine-minute mark, giving Tyler Kolek an unusually early appearance. With Jalen out, the visitors went on a 12-0 run. The backup guard was terrific in his first-half play, dishing five dimes in seven minutes, a third of the team’s total, and leading a second unit that tallied 17 first-half points.

A game of runs! Minny responded with a 13-2 run that included Ball attacking the paint for points and Jaden McDaniels swishing from long range. McDaniels was Minnesota’s most efficient scorer in the half, putting up 11 points on perfect 4-of-4 shooting, including three triples (but also three costly turnovers). Returning the favor, Josh Hart dropped a triple that started an 11-3 run and gave New York a 33-26 lead at the break.

In the second quarter, KAT and OG Anunoby stepped further into the spotlight. They combined for 30 first-half points on 12-of-18 shooting. Karl sang beautifully on his former home court, scoring 17 points and hauling in eight boards in just 16 minutes; OG chimed in with 13 points and a pair of blocks. Jose Alvarado got a little run but was quiet in the quarter. In a nice return to form, Josh Hart added nine points on 3-of-4 shooting from deep, while steady-eddie Landry Shamet provided a major lift off the bench with 10 points and a team-best plus-17 in 17 minutes.

The T’Wolves have length that can really clog the lane, and that explains why Jalen Brunson managed just seven points on 2-of-8 shooting, with his two makes coming from the outfield. Against most teams, Cap performs his string music in the paint, but these Minnesota trees make for a dense forest. Also underwhelming: Mikal Bridges, who threw the ball at the basket just once in his 11 minutes before intermission. It’s sort of wild that the Knicks posted 65 first-half points despite getting only nine points from their starting backcourt.

Also weird: Rudy Gobert had just five points and one rebound in his first 15 minutes. In fact, the Wolves’ starting frontcourt of McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga, and Gobert combined for two rebounds. Believe it, Ripley! They weren’t the only stinkers on the home team. Ball, Kuminga, and Ayo Dosunmu combined to shoot 4-of-17 through the half. Minnesota shot a respectable 44% overall and 39% from three, but outside of McDaniels, nobody found much rhythm. With the Knicks shooting a blistering 57% from the field and an eye-popping 63% from deep (10-of-16), the good guys were ahead 65-50 at intermission.

In the third quarter, Brunson shouldered the load, scoring 14 points in the period, and Bridges showed up to sink a three and commit two thefts. Towns continued to crash the glass but cooled off somewhat offensively, as did OG. For the home team, Kuminga poured in 14 points, making two three-pointers while blocking three shots. The Wolves couldn’t put together a sustained run, though. Trailing 83-66 with around 3:30 left, they outscored our heroes 12-7, cutting the score to 90-78 at the break.

To start the final frame, Kolek converted a four-point play to give the guests a 16-point lead. But we never thought the Furballs would roll over and die—and no, they didn’t. As New York’s offense stalled (e.g., Towns missed four of five, which he redeemed with three stuffs), McDaniels, Trey Lyles, and the Wolves chipped away at the lead. After New York went ahead 97-85 with 7:56 remaining, Minnesota scored eight unanswered points, including a McDaniels three and a Ball pull-up triple, to cut the lead to four. The Knicks went nearly four minutes without scoring, prompting a timeout and the return of Bridges and Anunoby.

What makes tonight’s win most stunning is that New York managed to achieve it despite going scoreless over the final 3:26. During that grisly stretch, KAT copped a flopping tech, Gobert slammed an alley-oop, and Ayo buried a three, bringing the Timberwolves within three with 2:34 left. Brunson missed a pull-up jumper, New York committed a shot-clock violation, Towns was called for an offensive foul with 1:04 left, and Bridges missed a turnaround jumper with 23 seconds remaining.

The hosts had plenty of chances to tie or steal the lead but couldn’t capitalize. Ball bricked two shots in the final 1:39; Dosunmu whiffed a bunny; and Bridges blocked Gobert’s putback attempt with 44 seconds left—arguably the biggest defensive play of the game. Ball blanked on a potential tying longball with 10 seconds remaining, and Kuminga collected the rebound but threw the ball away, with Landry Shamet securing the steal to end Minnesota’s night.

For those keeping track at home, the Timberwolves missed their final six field-goal attempts and committed five turnovers over the last five minutes. That’s a lot of ugly basketball to taint what was otherwise a quite pleasant viewing experience. But a win’s a win! And this one came over a very worthy opponent.

The Knicks host the Blazers on Saturday. Mo is sewing arms and legs onto your recap. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

items.content:
Fresh off a sweep over the border, the Knicks’ (8-6) championship parade makes a stop in Minnesota to face the Timberwolves (11-4) at Target Center. items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘It’s going to be bittersweet’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Revenge game for KAT today?

I don’t think so, but who knows.

Here’s the latest before visiting the Wolves in still-not-overly-cold Minnesota.

On Rick Brunson’s decision to bring Jose Alvarado into the game against Toronto:

“Just a great call. Rick Brunson made the call of throwing Jose in to see if he can give us a spark. So, just a heckuva call by Rick Brunson and just a fantastic job by Jose producing on both sides of the ball when his name was called.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns improving his passing decisions and avoiding risks:

“It’s a fine balance because he’s capable of making some beautiful passes in tight windows so you want to let him be him. But I thought earlier in the year — and we talked to him about it, and said it a couple times — he was trying to make the home-run pass a little too much.

“And he’s gotten to a point where he’s mixing it up now. We’re going to trust him because he’s obviously done it for many years now with good results. We’ll lean on him quite a bit in that regard but if we turn the ball over too much, we’ll let him know.”

On Towns’ basketball intelligence and ability to read the game:

“KAT’s got tremendous feel. He’s a smart, smart dude when it comes to a lot of things, but especially when it comes to the game of basketball.”

On Towns’ coachability and the impact of assistant coaches Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman:

“It’s easy to see where he is, because everything we’ve asked him to do, he’s tried to do. So, you’re extremely coachable. You got a great feel. And you got two guys in (assistant coaches) Brendan O’Connor and Darren Erman that are teaching you the game defensively at a really high level, and you’re starting to see the results of it.”

On the Knicks’ execution and contributions throughout the roster against Toronto:

“Our execution was at an extremely high level. We had a lot of guys contribute in a lot of ways tonight.”

On the Knicks early-season woes:

“It’s still a work in progress.”

On why the NBA must continue penalizing dangerous closeouts and landing-space violations after Brunson’s injury scare:

“They got to keep track of it because it’s going to happen. Everybody wants to try to block [Brunson’s] shot and every other guy’s shot. Some guys go forward too much and, if they do, there’s got to be a heavy penalty. Because if there’s no heavy penalty, then guys won’t be conscious of it. They’ll just keep sliding underneath guys.”

On why his shooting technique sometimes exposes him to dangerous situations:

“I fade a little bit. Taller guys are usually guarding me, so I got to be able to fade a little bit. Sometimes they’re not jumping straight up. They’re jumping towards me. It happens.”

On prioritizing getting buckets over worrying about landing on a defender’s foot:

“I’m not worried about falling on his foot. I’m more worried about if he’s close enough to block it. If he is too close, I probably won’t shoot it. If he’s not, ball is going up.”

On the Knicks rediscovering their preferred style of play against Toronto:

“We just played to the best of our abilities. I know the early season hasn’t looked like it, but that’s how we’re most comfortable.”

On the disappointment of not winning a championship during his nine seasons in Minnesota:

“I wanted to win one there. I didn’t accomplish that. But it was great to have those moments, to bring Minnesota back to the playoffs and be able to do a lot of things.”

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

“It’s going to be bittersweet. I’m just happy that I have such amazing fans and had such an amazing time in Minnesota. I love it to death. I love that place so it’s going to be cool to go back.”

On becoming a minority owner of Napoli’s basketball team:

“Napoli is a great underdog story and reminds me of what we have built with the Knicks in many ways. It is a project built around hard work, big dreams and the incredible passion Napoli fans have for their team. I’ve been coming to Naples and the Amalfi Coast for years, and I know what a fan base like this can mean to a team. Seeing this club already making noise in the EuroCup tells you where it’s headed.

“Matt Rizzetta and the team at Underdog Global Partners have high ambitions with a real plan for where this club is going. The Napoli journey is still very much in the first quarter, so I am excited to be a part of building this into something truly special in the years ahead.”

On Instagram after being demoted from starting center to the second unit:

“Nobody gone save me, gotta save my damn self.”

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks at Timberwolves, November 19, 2026
items.author: Kento Kato
items.content:
It wasn’t long ago that a Knicks vs. Timberwolves matchup almost felt like a mini-rivalry—one of the few the Knicks had against a team from the Western Conference.

Given the East Coast vs. West Coast of it all, and the LeBron vs. New York effect, the Lakers made for a fun matchup. The Spurs and Knicks have had some tough battles, including the 1999 Finals and the 2024 Christmas Day game, and that pseudo-rivalry was elevated to a new level with the 2026 Finals. But whenever the Knicks and Timberwolves played each other over the last two seasons, it felt like there was more on the line than just the game. It was a battle for narrative, not just bragging rights. Which team won the Karl-Anthony Towns trade? How would former Knicks Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo play against their former team? Now, with the Knicks having won a championship and Randle moving from Minnesota to Brooklyn, this matchup no longer feels as personal.

That doesn’t mean that it’ll be a bad game. Nor does it mean that the Timberwolves won’t be a tough opponent. At 11-4, they enter Thursday night with a better record than the Knicks despite being without star guard Anthony Edwards since he underwent knee surgery on October 29. And contrary to expectations, their success hasn’t been a result of LaMelo Ball putting up insane offensive numbers. Their scoring has been incredibly balanced, with Ayo Dosunmu averaging 18.6 PPG, Ball averaging 17.7 PPG, and Jaden McDaniels averaging 17.1 PPG. Even without a single player averaging more than 20 PPG, they’ve managed to have the 12th-highest offensive rating.

Where they’ve remained elite Edwards, though, is on the defensive end. The Timberwolves, thanks in large part to four-time Defensive Player of the Year winner Rudy Gobert, have been incredibly dominant defensively. As of today, they have the best defensive rating in the league at 104, two full points better than the second-place Celtics. They rank third in the league in opponents’ field goal percentage, first in opponents’ three-point percentage, and force the sixth-most turnovers per game.

The Knicks, who haven’t completely gotten past their early-season shooting struggles, may have a tough time scoring against the Timberwolves. Even with the recent play of Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Landry Shamet, and Miles McBride supplementing Karl-Anthony Towns’ dominant season, the Knicks still find themselves outside the top 10 in three-point percentage and near the bottom of the league in field goal percentage. That doesn’t mean the Knicks won’t be able to score, though. They have two very clear advantages heading into tonight.

One advantage is that they’ll have the two best players on the court. The Knicks can say this in a lot of games, and that hasn’t stopped them from getting off to a disappointing 8-6 start. And this matters less in the regular season than it does in the postseason. But this should still bode well for the Knicks. Brunson won Eastern Conference Player of the Week to kick off November and hasn’t really looked back. Even against a tough Raptors defense, he came through and put together back-to-back quality games. And you can make the argument that Towns hasn’t had a single game this season where he hasn’t been great in one way or another. The big man has also had some monstrous games against his former team, averaging 29.0 PPG, 14.3 RPG, and 3.7 APG while shooting 61.7% from the field and 56.3% from three. And in two of those three games, Towns scored 32 or more points and grabbed 13 or more rebounds.

The Knicks’ second advantage comes on the offensive boards. The Timberwolves give up the 12th-most offensive rebounds per game. Some of that is a direct result of their defense forcing so many misses. But with the Knicks being a top-five offensive rebounding team, Towns, as well as Andre Drummond and even Jordan Clarkson, could have big nights on the boards, making up for what could be an inefficient shooting night.

This will be a good test for a Knicks team that has earned seven of its eight wins against teams that are .500 or worse. The Timberwolves are 7-2 at home, deploy a dominant defense predicated on forcing players into the rim-protecting monster that is Gobert, and have a balanced offense that often scores just enough points. But expect the Knicks to lean on their two big horses. Brunson has also had some nice games against the Timberwolves and LaMelo Ball-led teams. And Towns has dominated just about everybody this season. We also can’t forget that the Knicks themselves have a good defense, which could test a limited Timberwolves offense. The Knicks come away with a low-scoring, ugly win led by Towns to improve to 9-6.

Who: New York Knicks (8-6) at Minnesota Timberwolves (11-4)Date: Thursday, November 19, 2026Place: Target Center, Minneapolis, MNFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: The longest single-opponent winning streaks in Knicks history
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
On Tuesday night, the Knicks outlasted the Raptors for the second time in three nights to extend a staggering 15-game winning streak against their Canadian rivals that dates back to January 2023.

Beyond the fact that it means that old friends RJ Barrett and Immanuel Quickley have never beaten their old team, it also extends one of the longest streaks in program history against a single opponent.

Celtics, 21 games (1993-98)

As mentioned on last night’s broadcast, it’s hard to believe such a dominant stretch existed against a longtime rival that has been the Eastern Conference’s banner of success for generations.

Simply, the sport is cyclical, and the few times the Celtics were in the doldrums, the Knicks were contending for titles. Through the many dark ages of Knicks history, the Celtics dominated. It’s why they’ve only faced off in the postseason three times in the last 35 years.

From 1965-67, the Celtics won 21 in a row against the Knicks in the heart of the Bill Russell era. It took 25 years to return the favor.

On January 10, 1993, the Celtics outlasted the Knicks at TD Garden in a 100-97 win. They wouldn’t win another game in this rivalry for over five years.

The Celtics won 48 games in 1992-93, but quickly fell into the East’s cellar. They wouldn’t win 40 games again in a season until 2001-02, while at the same time, Patrick Ewing and the Knicks had only the Bulls and Pacers competing with them for spots in the NBA Finals yearly.

Ewing would score 65 combined over the next two meetings in April 1993 before scoring 30 again on Opening Night that October in a three-point win in Boston. He routinely owned the Celtics during this time, reaching a crescendo with a 36-14 effort in March 1994.

As the Celtics got worse, the Knicks took advantage of them more and more. A 35-point blowout in February 1994 still stands as one of the biggest blowouts in the rivalry’s history. Hubert Davis nailed five threes and scored 25 points in a 90-83 win the following month.

It was always a different enemy that flummoxed the Celtics. Charles Smith scoring 25, Anthony Mason scoring 21, and John Starks and Ewing’s consistency. Even as Pat Riley turned into Jeff Van Gundy, the Knicks never lost a step.

The streak had reached 17 by January 28, 1997, when the pitiful 9-30 Celtics put the greatest scare into the contending Knicks yet. An eight-point lead in the final minutes dwindled to a tie on a Todd Day three in the final minute before free throws by Antoine Walker gave Boston the lead in the final minute.

Just when the streak appeared over, Chris Childs called game with eight seconds left.

Eventually, the streak would finally end on January 26, 1998, when the Knicks were held to just 85 points behind a 25-point gem by Chauncey Billups. Even this triumphant victory came with an asterisk, as Ewing missed the game due to wrist surgery. Huh.

Cavaliers, 18 games (1980-83)

The Knicks own the Cavs in the playoffs, but did you know there was a stretch they owned them like

In five all-time playoff meetings, the Knicks are 16-2 against the Cavs, but once took things to another level in the early 1980s.

Unlike the Celtics, this is pretty peculiar. The Knicks were an average team during this streak, but took advantage of one of the worst eras of Cavs basketball under Ted Stepien.

Quite precisely, this streak can be known as the “Stepien Streak”, as while he was owner from April 1980 to his sale in April 1983, the Cavs went 1-16 against the Knicks, with the lone win coming just two weeks before he sold the team in late March of 1983.

Highlights of the streak include Mike Glenn’s 29-point game in November 1980 (second-highest scoring game of his career), Ray Williams’ 37-point gem in an overtime win two weeks later, and perennially playing in front of 4,000 fans at an empty Richfield Coliseum. The NBA was totally different in the 80s.

Bullets, 17 games (1952-53)

Back in the day, there weren’t many teams. As such, you get stuff like this.

Over a span of 400 days from February 6, 1952, to March 11, 1953, the Knicks played the Baltimore Bullets 17 times and won every single one of them.

The 1950s Knicks can sometimes be referred to as the Silver Era of Knicks basketball due to the team making multiple Finals appearances before Russell came and made the East his own, so it’s no surprise they were dominant. But like this?

The lore of 1950s NBA is quite fascinating. These teams played each other three times in six days in February 1952 when the streak began, but played the games in three different places. The Bullets won 82-81 in the Baltimore Coliseum on February 4, the Knicks won 73-70 at the 69th Regiment Armory on February 6, and the two teams met in Philadelphia on February 8 in a 20-point blowout win for Ray Lumpp and the Knicks.

On March 5, the teams participated in a doubleheader at the Boston Garden, preceding a game between the Bucks and Celtics later that night.

In 1952-53, when the Knicks went 10-0 against the Bullets en route to a Finals appearance, they played one game in Philly, two games in Boston (one of which went to triple overtime), and even played in Trenton, New Jersey, on March 5, 1953.

Finally, the Bullets snapped the skid on November 14, 1953, behind 19 points by Max Zaslofsky in Baltimore.

Just for the hell of it, here’s some other weird neutral site locations from the 1950s:

  • January 29, 1952, in Louisville (vs. Indianapolis Olympians)
  • February 3, 1953, in Buffalo (vs. Milwaukee Hawks)
  • February 18, 1953, in Providence (vs. Boston Celtics)
  • January 22, 1954, in New Haven, CT (vs. Philadelphia Warriors)
  • Several times in 1954-55 in Miami (vs. Fort Wayne Pistons)
  • November 18, 1954, in Syracuse (vs. Philadelphia Warriors)
  • March 3, 1955, in Saratoga Springs (vs. Milwaukee Hawks)
  • March 13, 1956, in Moorhead, MN (vs. Minneapolis Lakers)
  • January 17, 1957, in Lacrosse, WI (vs. Minneapolis Lakers)
  • January 14, 1958, in St. Louis (vs. Cincinnati Royals)
  • February 21, 1958, in Camden, NJ (vs. Philadelphia Warriors)
  • January 22, 1962, in Moline, IL (vs. Chicago Packers)
  • March 12, 1962, in Seattle (vs. Los Angeles Lakers)
  • Various times in Hershey, PA (including the Wilt 100 game)

Pistons, 16 games (2020-24)

We’ve seen a new standard of excellence for the Knicks since the turn of the decade, They have three of these streaks in the last six years!

Back when the Pistons weren’t the annoying playoff contenders we know them as now, they were pretty damn awful. For years, it was a running joke that the COVID-19 pandemic was younger than the last Pistons win over the Knicks.

The streak began on February 8, 2020, when the Knicks overcame an early double-digit deficit to outlast the Pistons in Detroit in a battle of two lowly teams that wouldn’t even be invited to the bubble. Another win on March 8 would mark the team’s final home game with fans for another year due to the pandemic.

As the Knicks ascended, the Pistons stayed bad. On April 4, 2021, the Knicks eviscerated them by a 125-81 margin, the second-biggest blowout in the over 430 games in this matchup.

Even as the meltdown in 2021-22 ensued, the orange and blue survived a scare that March when Marvin Bagley III dropped 27, only for Alec Burks to strip Cade Cunningham in the final seconds to hold on.

The most memorable game of the streak came at the end. Facing the 8-48 Pistons at home in late February, the Knicks came out sleepy and watched as Cunningham nearly dragged his hapless team to the finish line to end the skid at 14, but shenanigans ensued with Donte DiVincenzo to somehow pull it off with a Josh Hart and-1.

Was it a foul? Does anyone really care?

The streak ended on December 7, 2024. We didn’t know it at the time, but the Pistons had finally emerged as threats, and they’d start their own six-game regular-season winning streak against the Knicks that lasted until three weeks ago.

Raptors and Nets, 15 games (active)

The last time the Raptors beat the Knicks? January 22, 2023.

The last time the Nets beat the Knicks? January 28, 2023.

The next opportunity for both to beat the Knicks? Brooklyn gets another chance on December 27, while Toronto next gets a crack on January 20. It’ll be basically four years for both since their last win.

These two streaks are tied for the fourth-longest active streaks in the NBA.

The three longer? OKC over Memphis, Cleveland over Washington, and the Clippers over the Hornets, all at 17. If you thought four years was a lot, it’s been almost 10 since the Hornets beat the Clippers!

These two streaks are very different, but also the same. Both teams have been worse than the Knicks this entire time, sometimes considerably worse, and have yielded some ugly blowouts.

There have also been plenty of scares. There’s the Brunson game-winner in the NBA Cup, the KAT heroics in The Six, the times that Brooklyn puts up a fight but folds late at Barclays Center, and the multiple double-digit comebacks we saw this week.

Either way, those are two Atlantic Division rivals that can’t beat the Knicks. It also comes directly after both dominated the Knicks for prolonged periods.

Remember Nic Claxton’s comments? Well, at the time, the Knicks were 0-9 against the Nets from 2020-23.

The Raptors went a blistering 23-5 against the Knicks from January 2016 to November 2023.

Ain’t no fun when the rabbit’s got the gun.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘The cardiac Knicks find a way’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The same we thought we’d never see GTA VI hit the proverbial shelves…

Here’s a bunch of quotes and comments coming off another Knicks dub in Toronto.

On Darko Rajaković’s coaching and the Raptors’ defensive intensity:

“Darko does a heckuva job… those guys play hard, really good defensively, give us fits.”

On Jalen Brunson’s late four-point play creating the separation needed to beat Toronto:

“That created the separation that we needed to be able to put them away. So just a big shot. It was one of those things where the play broke down, and we kept looking for an opportunity while spacing the floor. And Jalen found one and let it fly.”

On the Knicks’ late-game execution and contributions from Towns, Anunoby, Bridges and Shamet:

“I thought our execution, especially down the stretch, the last few minutes of the game, was at a pretty high level, on both ends of the floor, but particularly offensively. Our pacing, our spacing, our screening — we took care of the basketball down the stretch.

“We got a lot of different guys that produced in a lot of different ways tonight. Obviously, KAT continues to be a double-double machine. OG [Anunoby] was our defensive player of the game. … Mikal was good for us, especially down the stretch. And Landry Shamet was huge.”

On his improved relationship with Karl-Anthony Towns and the importance of adapting his coaching philosophy:

“It’s just part of being around each other. You hope your relationship with everybody grows. That’s not gonna always happen but you hope it does. KAT’s got a really good feel of how to play the game. Obviously he’s a perennial All-Star. So those things you’ve always got to take into account when it comes to trying to listen or try to adapt more to what their style of play is.

“As a head coach — come in, it’s your first year, and you have an idea what you want to do. Sometimes it doesn’t fit. Offensively, or defensively. And that’s when you’ve got to pivot. And so we kept pivoting and pivoting and building until we found a nice little groove. We feel pretty good about each other right now.”

On recovering from the ankle injury scare after his four-point play:

“Adrenaline was pumping, and went back out there.”

On Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges regaining confidence and contributing to the Knicks’ success:

“This is a huge night for them, the way they played. They’re gaining confidence every single night. They’re going to continue to do great things for us and they’re only going to get better.”

On the Knicks rediscovering their ability to win close games:

“A lot of times when we get in games like that, especially last year, the cardiac Knicks find a way.”

On gaining Mike Brown’s trust and having more input in the team’s strategy:

“It’s more familiarity with the system and building that trust with Mike where he can trust me with things I see and say, which started in the playoffs. So building off that this year. Having more input and him hearing me out.”

On acting as a second coach and collaborating with Brown during games:

“Him trusting me like a second coach. Me and him are always coaching with each other in the game, looking at game plans and plays and maybe ideologies and things I see that can help our team win, especially in close games. Working with him and coaching on the floor. It’s been great. It’s been fun.”

On how his relationship with Brown has improved since the championship run:

“We just grew. We’ve grown with each other. And obviously there’s trust that has to be established and both of us trust each other a lot. And the last playoff run showed it. So just building off that trust and the relationship that was built in the playoffs and having it make our team better this year.”

On Jose Alvarado’s professionalism and importance to the Knicks’ locker room:

“Jose is a consummate professional. He’s probably one of the best locker room guys we have, and one of the best people we have on the bench. His energy, just his presence, with a jersey on or a warmup on, it means more for this team than what the stats show.”

On his recent mental struggles:

“Has been kicking my ass for a couple weeks.”

On stepping up his game on Tuesday after struggling through a few games:

“I think it was a step in the right direction. I think I’m obviously getting into the flow, into the rhythm of things, but today was a step in the right direction. Still a lot to improve on, but you got to start stacking days at some point.”

On how his contract situation can amplify the pressure of poor performances:

“That’s a low-hanging fruit. Sometimes some of those things amplify because you’re in a contract year, essentially. It’s human nature.

“It’s in the back of your mind, and when you start focusing on those things, negative outcomes happen.”

On trying to overcome his struggles and improve his mindset:

“When you’re in the middle of it, there’s not much that can really help. At the end of the day, you just have to go out there. And I think today I had a little bit of a better spirit.”

On the negative thought patterns that have affected his performances:

“I’m struggling to shoot the ball, but it’s one of those things where you start looking at the negatives and that’s all you see. You don’t see some of the positives. Then it’s a snowball effect. One thing happens and you’re trying to get yourself out of a hole that you’re not giving yourself the ability to get out of. It’s about playing with that joyful spirit, looking at things half full instead of half empty.”

On dealing with physical and mental challenges simultaneously:

“For me, this (rough patch) is a little harder because I’m trying to get the mental aspect right and the physical aspect right. It can be easier when you’re just dealing with one of those things. … I’m battling both of those things. I’m trying to give myself a little bit of grace with that.”

On maintaining a positive attitude despite losing his place in the Knicks’ rotation:

“I think it’s more how I was raised [by] my parents. Treat people how you want to be treated. Sometimes the situation isn’t going to be what you want. You can’t control certain things and control what you can and that’s your attitude, your energy every day. So I try to do that.

“I’m human, I have days where it’s not going to be all lovey-dovey. But I always tell myself, ‘Whether I’m not playing or not, I got the best seats in the house.’ And I get to support my teammates. So I try to go with that mindset as best I can and my teammates allow me to be myself.”

On the viral clip showing him comforting Mikal Bridges on the bench:

“[Mikal] is fine. We are all human. The camera caught us that time, but I probably do stuff like that 100 times during a game.”

On staying prepared for opportunities after falling out of the rotation:

“The season is long. I’ve been on the other side. When I first got in the league [in 2021], I wasn’t even touching the court. Then eventually I got to touch the court and get some reps in and played a huge role in the rotation.

“Sometimes you get out of it. The only way to get back is stay ready because an opportunity is going to come, you just don’t know when. So that’s the hardest thing is the guessing game of when that will happen. But you work, work and work and trust that it will come in the end of the day.”

On how close the Raptors came to beating the Knicks in their previous meeting:

“After rewatching and rewatching and rewatching film, we played against the NBA champions and, in my three-and-a-half years here as coach, that’s when we came the closest to beating them. We’re getting better. Just one free throw and the game is completely different.”

items.title: Knicks 111, Raptors 102: “Let it be 15 straight”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
One of the more prominent flies caught in the interwebs these days was the nomination of Robert Pattinson as the new lead for the James Bond franchise. Yes, the guy who made daughters melt by the millions about two decades ago and who always looks like the vampire that made him prominent drank all the blood from his veins. Apparently he’s a really good actor, but pardon me if I’m not acting like I’m some kind of wannabe film critic just because I like movies every once in a while.

For my liking, the 007 I loved ended with the retirement of Roger Moore, a second gut punch not needed after the grim realization that Sean Connery’s time in Her Majesty’s Service was over (we ignore Roger Lazenby for obvious reasons). Before watching any of the newer films, I always much rather flopped in one of the classics, because with the world spinning faster every day, there are just some things in life I’d like to stay the way they are. Like that bank account from December before all the insurance companies wish you a happy new year or that favorite dish your Grandma used to make before she discovered light whipping cream. And while we’re at it, the fact that the New York Knicks do not lose to the Toronto Raptors.

Knicks work their late-game magic – again

After watching the Knicks almost win a carbon copy of their game on Sunday in Toronto for their 15th in a row against the Dinos, it truly feels like some divine decree puts some prehistoric panic on the Raptors in the final minutes and sprinkles just enough calmness on the orange and blue to pull it out in the end. Just like Unmitigated Gall wrote in the celebratory Postgame Thread: “Sayeth the Lord: Let it be 15 straight”. But maybe it’s also just pure and legit NBA talent taking over, and prevailing over the guys who are airballing free throws or thought it was a good idea to give Jakob Poeltl north of 100 million dollars to play basketball.

Even if Jalen Brunson shot it as purely as “The Man with the Golden Gun,” late everything for New York started and ended last night with Karl-Anthony Towns. Early in the season, he looks sharper than Oddjob’s razor-edged hat (shoutout to “Tosh Togo” Harold Sakata) and, on top of it, more powerful than Richard Kiel’s “Jaws”. KAT’s dominance was on full display against a team that could only put defenders on him who were either too small or too slow. Dismantling those adversaries wasn’t even the most impressive thing the 31-year-old did, as his passing at times was as beautiful as Honey Ryder, Tatiana Romanova and Miss Galore combined.

To be serious for a second: It is astonishing how Karl-Anthony Towns has turned around his career after more than a decade in the league. He is by far the most consistent Knick right now, has cut down on his foul issues for the time being, and looks extremely decisive on both ends of the court. In Minnesota, he always gave the impression of lacking professionalism, and now he looks like the most serious player on a team full of guys who seemingly laughed the last time the Raptors or Nets beat the Knicks. Maybe “You only live twice” as a basketball player, but in KAT’s case that looks to be plenty enough.

Karl-Anthony Towns shines for New York

The “License to Kill” in the end, of course, rests with his buddy about a foot shorter than him. You wouldn’t believe it watching the first half last night as the Raptors’ eyes got as wide seeing Jalen Brunson defend them as Auric Goldfinger’s were when he saw that shiny gold bar on the 18th green at Stoke Park. If there was a possession where Toronto didn’t attack Brunson in the first half, I seriously cannot remember it. The same goes for any offensive possession that didn’t end up with a late shot clock. It was really a desperate look at times, so desperate that Mike Brown even turned to a zone in the second half, called blitzes when Toronto barely crossed midcourt, and gave sparkplug Jose Alvarado the nod late in the third quarter. And as so often in the past, some of that stuff worked (we still do not like those traps, Mikey).

With the game on the line, the Knicks turned into a rolling “Thunderball” that just couldn’t be stopped. Mikal Bridges locked down on defense for the second straight game, the backup point guard duelists provided numerous little plays, OG Anunoby smiled, and Landry Shamet once again looked like some cool device Q designed in an underground bunker – the red button unleashes movement threes and hellish defense on the opponent. And you have to deal with KAT and Brunson on top of all that? Good luck. When the orange and blue have it going like that, it seems as if they could even make some of those megalomaniac Bond villain plots for world supremacy work. Everything seems possible – even the Captain swatting shots and turning into Jalen Dikembe Mutombo Mpolondo Mukamba Jean-Jacques Wamutombo Brunson. RIP to the legend.

Since “Diamonds Are Forever,” we really do not need a constant reminder of everything these Knicks are capable of; we still remember last year pretty well. That doesn’t mean it does not feel extremely awesome and puts a comfortable calm into a fan’s heart to see them clicking on all cylinders. It would be nice if these cylinders wouldn’t take three quarters to get going, but as long as the Knicks go home with goddess Victory, there’s nothing wrong with things the way they are. Just like there probably is nothing wrong with Robert Pattinson playing James Bond, so let us all wish him well.

And let’s hope for him he’s not a Raptors fan.
